# Abstract

Between the handover of Dutch West New Guinea to Indonesia in 1962–1963 and Papua New Guinea's fifty-year post-independence census milestone in 2024–2025, the world's largest tropical island underwent the fastest sustained demographic expansion in Oceania [@repository1982population; @guinea20252024; @indonesia2021hasil]. Across 28 modern first-level administrative units occupying 1.007.772,1 km² of raster mask area—Papua New Guinea's 22 provinces including the National Capital District and the Autonomous Region of Bougainville (555.519,7 km²) alongside the six post-2022 provinces of Indonesian Papua (452.252,6 km²)—harmonised island population more than tripled in forty-five years from 4,43M in 1980 to 7,61M in 2000, 10,49M in 2010 and 15,64M (15.642.529, density 15,52 inhabitants per km²) at closing in 2025, compounding at 2,84% per annum across 1980 to 2025. East of the 141st meridian, Papua New Guinea expanded almost entirely through high rural fertility and falling mortality from 2,18M in 1966 and 3,01M in 1980 to 5,19M in 2000, 7,28M in 2011 and 10,19M in the official 2024 provincial returns (10,02M in the constant-boundary provincial ledger), anchored by dense Highland sweet-potato basins and rapid informal urbanisation in Port Moresby (756,8k) and Lae (148,9k in 2011) despite persistent census undercount and overcount disputes [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20132011; @tatem2022high]. West of the border, Indonesian Papua grew even faster—compounding at 3,53% per annum from 923,4k in 1971 to 2,21M in 2000, 3,59M in 2010 and 5,62M in 2023—through a dual engine pairing state *transmigrasi* and spontaneous archipelagic migration into coastal hubs (Jayapura 414,9k, Sorong 295,8k, Timika 148,9k, Merauke 108,5k, Nabire 104,3k and Manokwari 102,4k) with Indigenous Papuan demographic resilience across the highland provinces of Papua Pegunungan (1,46M) and Papua Tengah (1,36M) [@elmslie2010west; @ananta2016statistics; @pona2012transmigrasi]. Across 145 catalogued settlements and 424 dated observations, the island urban hierarchy follows a tight Zipf distribution ($\alpha = 1,13$, $R^2 = 0,98$ across the upper 72 centres) spanning dual national capitals, mining towns and highland administrative stations.

# Background

## Political Partition at the 141st Meridian and Late Colonial Thresholds (1962 to 1975)

Modern New Guinea opened in geopolitical divergence along the straight north–south border surveyed at 141° east longitude. In the western half, the New York Agreement of August 1962 transferred Dutch Netherlands New Guinea via a brief United Nations Temporary Executive Authority to the Republic of Indonesia on 1 May 1963, formalised through the contested 1969 Act of Free Choice (*Penentuan Pendapat Rakyat*) [@elmslie2010west; @pona2012transmigrasi]. Renamed West Irian (*Irian Barat*) and from 1973 *Irian Jaya*, the western territory entered Indonesian administration with fewer than 900k inhabitants dispersed across coastal Bird's Head ports, Cenderawasih Bay islands, the southern alluvial marshes of Asmat and Merauke, and only recently contacted interior valleys of the Central Cordillera [@papua2011penduduk; @kamun2016kajian]. When Jakarta conducted its first nationwide enumeration to include the territory—Sensus Penduduk 1971—official returns recorded 923.440 residents, over 95% of them Indigenous Melanesian Papuans, with Hollandia (rechristened Sukarnapura and then Jayapura) holding just 45.786 inhabitants alongside Sorong (23.800), Manokwari (21.400), Biak (21.200) and Merauke (16.800) [@elmslie2010west; @ananta2016statistics].

Across the eastern half, Australia accelerated decolonisation of the joint Territory of Papua and New Guinea after 1964, granting internal self-government in December 1973 and full sovereign independence on 16 September 1975 [@repository1982population]. Australia's final colonial censuses of 1966 (2.184.986 total, including 2.150.317 Indigenous citizens and 34.669 non-Indigenous expatriates) and 1971 (2.489.935) revealed an overwhelmingly rural society in which over 90% of people lived by subsistence gardening, sago harvesting and smallholder cash cropping [@repository1982population; @bourke2009food]. Yet urban drift had already begun: Port Moresby nearly doubled from 41.848 in 1966 to 76.507 in 1971, Lae more than doubled from 16.546 to 38.707, and copper mining at Panguna on Bougainville spawned the brand-new company town of Arawa (5.039 in 1971, surging to 12.623 by 1980) alongside expanding Highland centres at Goroka (12.066) and Mount Hagen (10.621) [@repository1982population; @bakker1986mortality].

## Independent Papua New Guinea: Fertility Momentum, Resource Enclaves and Conflict (1975 to 2025)

Independence altered Papua New Guinea's administrative machinery without slowing its demographic engine. Expatriate Australian planters and civil servants departed steadily after 1975—partially offset in later decades by overseas Filipino technical professionals and a renewed wave of mainland Chinese commercial migrants in urban retail and resource services [@alvarez2005overseas; @chin2024chinese]—leaving national growth driven almost entirely by Indigenous natural increase [@repository1982population; @guinea2002papua]. Malaria suppression in coastal lowlands, rural aid-post expansion and vaccination campaigns had cut infant and child mortality substantially during the 1960s and 1970s, raising life expectancy from roughly 40 years in 1966 to nearly 50 by 1980 [@bakker1986mortality]. Fertility, however, declined only slowly: total fertility hovered above 5 births per woman through the 1980s, stood near 4,6 at the 2000 census and remained at 4,2 in the 2016–2018 Demographic and Health Survey—the highest sustained rate in the Pacific outside Timor-Leste [@guinea2002papua; @guinea2019papua].

At the same time, public health progress stalled unevenly across rugged interior valleys after 1980. Child mortality analyses and verbal autopsy surveillance demonstrate steep sub-national gaps between the National Capital District and Island provinces on one hand and remote Highland, Sepik and Gulf districts on the other, where under-five mortality remained above 70–90 per 1.000 live births and adult mortality stayed elevated through infectious diseases, maternal complications and rising non-communicable illness [@bauze2012equity; @kitur2019estimating; @kitur2020mortality; @hart2020mortality]. Despite stagnant health infrastructure, a very young age structure (over 38% under age 15 across most of the period) generated relentless population momentum, lifting national census returns from 3.010.727 in 1980 and 3.762.000 in 1990 to 5.190.786 in 2000, 7.275.324 in 2011 and 10,19M in the 2024 final provincial figures [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20132011; @guinea20252024].

Two severe shocks disrupted provincial trajectories inside independent PNG. First, disputes over landowners' royalties and environmental tailings from the Panguna copper mine ignited the Bougainville Crisis (1988–1998), a decade-long civil war and naval blockade that closed the mine permanently, prevented enumeration of North Solomons Province in the 1990 census (forcing a demographic projection of 154k), killed an estimated 10k to 20k people through combat and medical deprivation, emptied Arawa from 12.623 in 1980 to 2.217 in 2000, and shifted provincial administration to Buka (5.416 by 2011) before the 2001 Peace Agreement established the Autonomous Region of Bougainville [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20132011]. Second, on 19 September 1994, the twin volcanic vents of Tavurvur and Vulcan erupted across Blanche Bay in East New Britain, burying colonial Rabaul under metres of wet ash; Rabaul collapsed from 17.044 residents in 1990 (down from its 1971 peak of 26.619) to 3.907 in 2000, while provincial headquarters relocated permanently across the bay to Kokopo (rising from 3.152 in 1990 to 6.677 in 2011) [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20132011]. Elsewhere, extractive megaprojects created isolated frontier boomtowns—Ok Tedi copper-gold mining lifting Tabubil from bushland to 10.270 and river port Kiunga to 10.981 in Western Province, Porgera gold in Enga, Lihir gold at Londolovit in New Ireland, and the ExxonMobil PNG LNG project in Hela and Southern Highlands—yet household surveys show resource booms delivered remarkably limited broad-based gains to rural subsistence families, accelerating informal squatter migration toward Port Moresby and Lae [@guinea2011papua; @group2014papua; @baxi2024how].

## Indonesian West New Guinea: *Transmigrasi*, Spontaneous Migration and *Pemekaran* (1962 to 2025)

West of the 141st meridian, demographic transformation unfolded through a wholly different political economy. Under President Suharto's New Order (*Orde Baru*), Jakarta designated *Irian Jaya* a strategic frontier for agricultural colonisation and mineral extraction [@pona2012transmigrasi; @elmslie2010west]. State-sponsored *transmigrasi* schemes resettled tens of thousands of landless Javanese, Sundanese and Balinese farming families onto cleared lowland tracts around Jayapura (Arso and Koya), Nabire (such as Kampung Wadio in Nabire Barat), Manokwari (Prafi), Sorong (Aimas and Klamono) and Merauke [@pona2012transmigrasi; @mahmudah2023pemertahanan; @facultyoflaw2021transmigrati]. Even larger than official transmigration was spontaneous (*swakarsa*) chain migration by Bugis, Makassarese, Butonese, Madurese, Torajan and Moluccan traders, fishermen, drivers and construction workers drawn to expanding ports and markets across Sorong, Jayapura, Manokwari, Merauke and Fakfak [@saprillah2011migrasi; @anwar2016faktor; @ananta2016statistics].

Simultaneously, the opening of Freeport's Ertsberg (1972) and colossal Grasberg (1988) copper-gold mines in the Sudirman Range transformed southern Mimika Regency overnight: highland company town Tembagapura rose from 5.800 in 1980 to 23.022 in 2020, while lowland gateway Timika exploded twenty-three-fold from 6.500 in 1980 to 76.500 in 2000 and 148.900 in 2023, drawing both Indonesian migrants and Indigenous Amungme, Kamoro and central Highland workers [@papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil]. Following the 2001 Special Autonomy Law (*Otonomi Khusus*, Otsus), provincial governments gained statutory discretion over transmigration inflows, curtailing new Jakarta-directed agricultural blocks while spontaneous urban migration and high Indigenous fertility sustained rapid growth [@pona2012transmigrasi; @facultyoflaw2021transmigrati; @badanpusatstat2018indonesia].

Administratively, Jakarta subdivided unified *Irian Jaya* in two major waves of territorial proliferation (*pemekaran*). First, in 2003, the western Bird's Head and Bomberai peninsulas split off as *Irian Jaya Barat* (renamed *Papua Barat* in 2007), creating a two-province structure used in the 2010 and 2020 national censuses [@papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil]. Second, in July and December 2022, national legislation partitioned the two provinces into six: rump *Papua* (Jayapura, Biak, Yapen and Sarmi along the north coast), *Papua Barat* (Manokwari, Bintuni, Fakfak and Kaimana), *Papua Barat Daya* (Sorong, Raja Ampat and Maybrat), *Papua Tengah* (Nabire, Timika/Mimika and the Paniai–Puncak highland belt), *Papua Pegunungan* (the densely settled Baliem Valley and central highlands around Wamena) and *Papua Selatan* (Merauke, Asmat, Mappi and Boven Digoel) [@indonesia2021hasil; @kamun2016kajian]. Ethnic analysis of the 2010 census demonstrated the stark spatial bifurcation produced by half a century of dual growth: non-Papuan migrants and their descendants reached roughly half of the combined population—and strong majorities in coastal cities such as Jayapura, Sorong, Timika and Merauke—whereas Indigenous Papuans remained 85% to 98% of the population across the central cordillera of Papua Pegunungan and interior Papua Tengah [@ananta2016statistics; @elmslie2010west].

# Methodology

## Twenty-Eight-Province Constant-Boundary Partition Across Divided New Guinea

To track post-colonial population dynamics across the entire New Guinea archipelago without administrative breaks from *pemekaran* in Indonesia or provincial splits in Papua New Guinea, AUSTRAL adopts a 28-unit constant-boundary framework spanning 1.007.772,1 km² of rasterised landmass and coastal archipelago mask from 1962 to 2026. East of the 141st meridian, 22 sub-regions match Papua New Guinea's post-2012 provincial map (555.519,7 km²): the National Capital District (338,7 km²), Autonomous Region of Bougainville (16.226,8 km²), seven Highland provinces including Hela (split from Southern Highlands in 2012) and Jiwaka (split from Western Highlands in 2012), four Momase provinces (Morobe, Madang, East Sepik, West Sepik/Sandaun), five remaining Southern provinces (Central, Gulf, Milne Bay, Northern/Oro, Western) and four remaining New Guinea Islands provinces (East New Britain, West New Britain, New Ireland, Manus) [@guinea20132011; @guinea20252024]. West of the border, six sub-regions match Indonesia's post-2022 six-province partition (452.252,6 km²): Papua (95.291,9 km²), Papua Barat (73.323,5 km²), Papua Barat Daya (48.244,5 km²), Papua Pegunungan (55.566,5 km²), Papua Selatan (119.866 km²) and Papua Tengah (59.960,2 km²) [@indonesia2021hasil].

Mask areas represent rasterised coastal-and-island administrative envelopes including Bismarck, Admiralty, Milne Bay, Raja Ampat and Cenderawasih archipelago margins; consequently, they exceed dry-land cadastral survey totals modestly (roughly 463k km² dry land for PNG and 412k km² for Indonesian Papua against 555.519,7 km² and 452.252,6 km² mask footprints). All sub-regional density figures in this chapter therefore denote uniform mask-area densities (inhabitants per km²), preserving strict internal comparability across mainland and maritime provinces.

## Dual-Agency Census Harmonisation, Growth Rates and Back-Projection

Statistical reconstruction integrates two distinct national statistical series with differing enumeration calendars. For Papua New Guinea, primary provincial anchors derive from five post-independence National Statistical Office (NSO) censuses—1980, 1990, 2000, 2011 and 2024—supplemented by the 1966 and 1971 Australian Territory of Papua and New Guinea national enumerations and the 2009–2010 Household Income and Expenditure Survey plus 2016–2018 Demographic and Health Survey for vital-rate checks [@repository1982population; @guinea2002papua; @guinea2011papua; @guinea20132011; @guinea2019papua; @guinea20252024]. Because Hela and Jiwaka attained provincial status only in May 2012, official NSO retroactive district aggregations establish their 2000, 2011 and 2024 totals directly while pre-2000 HGIS reconstructions apportion their historical shares out of undivided Southern Highlands and Western Highlands [@guinea20132011]. For Indonesian Papua, official Badan Pusat Statistik (BPS) Sensus Penduduk returns for 1971, 1980, 1990, 1995 (SUPAS), 2000, 2010 and 2020 plus 2023 mid-year provincial registrations are reconciled to the six post-2022 provinces using regency (*kabupaten*) and municipality (*kota*) aggregates from SP2010, SP2020 and BPS 2023 provincial handbooks, with 1971 provincial shares back-apportioned proportionally from regency baselines [@papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil; @badanpusatstat2018indonesia].

Between bounding raw census anchors $t_1 < t < t_2$, harmonised decadal and quinquennial benchmark populations $P_j(t)$ for each province $j$ are derived via log-linear interpolation:

$$P_j(t) = P_j(t_1) \cdot \left(\frac{P_j(t_2)}{P_j(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{t - t_1}{t_2 - t_1}}$$

Compound annual growth rates across any intercensal or secular window $[t_1, t_2]$ follow:

$$g_j(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_j(t_2)}{P_j(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Outside observed provincial anchors—specifically prior to PNG's 1980 constant-boundary series (or 2000 for Hela and Jiwaka)—the provincial benchmark cache clamps pre-anchor years flat, whereas the gridded raster series back-projects every province smoothly to 1962 using national intercensal growth schedules so early-epoch totals remain demographically realistic.

## Four-Wave Urban Gazetteer Assembly and Zipf Scaling

Parallel to provincial aggregates, AUSTRAL compiles an evidence-based gazetteer of 145 settlements (92 in Papua New Guinea and 53 in Indonesian Papua) containing 424 dated observations (mean 2,92 observations per centre) spanning 1962 to 2024 with 0% crowd-sourced fallback. Ingestion followed four ledger-audited waves: Wave 1 extracted 137 urban and administrative town time series directly from PNG NSO censuses (1966–2024), BPS *Sensus Penduduk* and *Kabupaten Dalam Angka* reports (1971–2023) and late Dutch New Guinea administrative tables [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20132011; @papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil]; Wave 2 integrated 7 anthropological, mission-station and regional monograph centres (including highland and Sepik field settlements such as Tsembaga and Kanganaman) [@fyfe2009gender; @bourke2009food]; Wave 3 enforced strict settlement-vs-rural separation—excluding 299 Papua New Guinea Rural Local-Level Government (LLG) administrative divisions modelled strictly via areal masks and merging 12 duplicate alias entries within 25 km (such as Wakwak into Mendi); and Wave 4 closed with a single sub-region verification addition (0,69% marginal gain, zero empty sub-regions and zero unaccounted candidates). Upper-half rank-size scaling fits $\log_{10} P_{(r)} = a - \alpha \log_{10} r$ across the top 72 centres ($r = 1 \ldots 72$) to test whether dual-state partition distorts island-wide urban primacy.

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciling Benchmarks Against Censuses, HGIS and Gridded Models

Cross-validation against official national census summaries, the 122-row Historical GIS (HGIS) territorial panel (spanning 1980, 2000, 2010, 2020 and 2025) and the gridded raster series uncovers strong post-1980 agreement alongside three major statistical discrepancies that must be stated plainly rather than smoothed over. In 1980, total island population stands at 4,18M by adding official national censuses (3.010.727 PNG plus 1.173.875 *Irian Jaya*), 4,27M in the raster model and 4,27M across the 23-unit HGIS snapshot (3.092.886 PNG plus 1.173.875 unified *Irian Jaya*), versus 4,43M in the constant-boundary provincial benchmark table (elevated slightly because Hela and Jiwaka clamp their 2000 populations backward into 1980). By 2000, alignment tightens further: official censuses sum to 7,4M (5.190.786 PNG plus 2.213.833 Indonesian Papua), the raster series reads 7,31M, the HGIS snapshot reads 7,31M and the benchmark table reads 7,61M. By closing in 2023–2025, official counts sum to 15,81M (10,19M PNG in 2024 plus 5,62M Indonesian Papua in 2023), matching our 2025 benchmark of 15,64M within 1% and our 2025 HGIS panel (16,03M) within 1,4% [@guinea20252024; @indonesia2021hasil].

Three specific anomalies surface during audit and require explicit documentation. First, in the 28-province constant-boundary cache (and in the 1980 HGIS snapshot), Western Highlands carries the identical five-census sequence as Western Province (78.575 in 1980, 110.420 in 1990, 153.304 in 2000, 201.351 in 2011 and 300.019 in 2024), understating Western Highlands against official PNG NSO returns (265.656 in 1980 and 336.178 in 1990 undivided; 254.227 in 2000, 362.850 in 2011 and 462.566 in 2024 post-Jiwaka split) by roughly 162,5k inhabitants in 2024 [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20132011; @guinea20252024]. That single alignment offset explains virtually the entire gap between our 22-province PNG cache sum (10.022.816) and the official 2024 NSO national total (10.185.363, or 10,19M). Second, in the 2010 and 2020 HGIS snapshots (and consequently the 2010–2020 raster totals of 12,57M and 17,61M), the two-province *Papua* and *Papua Barat* HGIS polygons register inflated sums of 5,67M in 2010 and 8,61M in 2020—roughly 58% above official BPS SP2010 (3,59M) and SP2020 (5,44M) totals—reflecting double-counted transitional regency totals prior to the clean 2025 six-province BPS HGIS reconciliation (5,79M) [@papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil]. Third, prior to 1980, flat backward clamping in the constant-boundary benchmark table holds 1960–1970 artificially at 4,09M, whereas actual island population stood near 2,89M in 1962 and 3,41M in 1970 as captured by our back-projected raster series and early official censuses (2,49M PNG in 1971 plus 0,92M West Irian in 1971 = 3,41M) [@repository1982population; @elmslie2010west].

## Papua New Guinea Census Debate: Undercount, Overcount and Gridded Satellite Estimates

Few contemporary census series have provoked sharper methodological debate than Papua New Guinea's enumerations between 2011 and 2024 [@tatem2022high; @ige2023counting; @guinea20252024]. Logistical obstacles across roadless highland valleys, flooded Sepik plains and sprawling urban squatter settlements plagued both the 2011 census (which suffered delayed fieldwork and uneven post-enumeration checks) and the postponed 2024 count [@guinea20132011; @ige2023counting]. In 2022, a joint UNFPA and WorldPop satellite building-footprint modelling exercise estimated PNG's resident population at roughly 17M—nearly double the UN projection of 9,9M and far above the 10,19M later published by PNG NSO for 2024 [@tatem2022high; @guinea20252024].

Independent demographic checks favour the 10M–11M bracket over the 17M satellite outlier while still acknowledging localised under-enumeration in 2024. Compounding the well-audited 2000 census (5,19M) at the 2000–2011 intercensal rate of 3,1% per annum—or at the declining 2,5%–2,7% natural increase implied by the 2016–2018 DHS total fertility rate of 4,2 and persistent rural child and adult mortality—yields 10M to 11,4M inhabitants in 2024, never 17M [@guinea2002papua; @guinea2019papua; @kitur2019estimating]. Satellite building counts in Melanesia systematically over-predict population because rural households maintain multiple separate structures (cooking houses, men's houses, garden huts and abandoned bush-material dwellings) that optical algorithms classify as distinct residential units [@tatem2022high; @bourke2009food]. Conversely, fieldwork audits of PNG's 2024 census highlight real undercounting among floating urban populations, homeless residents and conflict-affected highland wards in Enga and Hela, alongside local political incentives in some districts to inflate electoral rolls [@ige2023counting; @guinea20252024]. Table \ref{tab:national-series} places the primary official census series for both halves of New Guinea side by side from 1966 to 2024.

# Results

## Island-Wide Demographic Surge (1962 to 2025)

Measured across both sovereign halves together, New Guinea experienced one of the most sustained half-century population expansions in the modern developing world, illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:ng-trajectory}. From 3,41M inhabitants on the 1971 official baseline (2,89M in the 1962 raster reconstruction), the island reached 4,18M official residents (4,43M benchmark) in 1980, 5,41M (5,67M) in 1990, 7,4M (7,61M) in 2000, 10,87M (10,49M) across 2010–2011 and 15,81M official residents (15,64M benchmark, mask density 15,52 inhabitants per km²) by 2023–2025 [@repository1982population; @guinea20252024; @indonesia2021hasil]. Unlike Polynesia, Micronesia or Fiji—where overseas emigration to New Zealand, Australia and the United States siphoned off substantial shares of natural increase—neither Papua New Guinea nor Indonesian Papua experienced mass international out-migration. Virtually every birth cohort remained inside the island, while Indonesian Papua absorbed substantial net in-migration from Java, Sulawesi and Maluku [@ananta2016statistics; @saprillah2011migrasi; @anwar2016faktor]. As a result, Indonesian Papua's share of total island population climbed steadily from 27,1% in 1971 and 28,1% in 1980 to 29,9% in 2000, 33,1% in 2010 and 35,6% by 2023–2024.

First stands the Highlands demographic core—seven compact intermontane provinces occupying barely 11,9% of PNG's mask area yet holding 3,47M inhabitants in our provincial ledger (and 3,63M using official Western Highlands returns, roughly 35,7% of the entire nation) in 2024 [@bourke2009food; @guinea20252024]. Intensive mounded sweet-potato (*Ipomoea batatas*) agriculture, cool malaria-free valleys between 1.400 m and 2.400 m elevation and smallholder Arabica coffee income sustained the highest rural densities anywhere in Oceania: Jiwaka (455,2k, density 76,12 per km²), Eastern Highlands (800,1k, up from 276,7k in 1980, density 66,99), Chimbu/Simbu (458,4k, density 53,19), Southern Highlands (602,1k, density 43,03), Enga (490k, density 38,73), Hela (365,8k, density 33,45) and Western Highlands (300k in the ledger; 462,6k official, giving over 140 per km² even on the ledger floor) [@bourke2009food; @guinea20132011]. High rural land pressure in Chimbu, Enga and Southern Highlands fuelled massive circular and permanent out-migration down the Highlands Highway to Lae, Port Moresby and West New Britain oil-palm estates [@group2014papua; @guinea2011papua].

Second stands Momase along the northern mainland littoral and Sepik–Ramu–Markham river basins—2,75M inhabitants (27,5% of the PNG ledger) in 2024. Morobe remained PNG's single most populous province at every census, climbing from 310,6k in 1980 to 539,4k in 2000, 674,8k in 2011 and 997,5k in 2024, anchored by industrial port Lae (148.934 in 2011) and inland Bulolo–Wau forestry and mining corridors [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20252024]. Adjacent Madang surged from 211,1k to 761,2k (density 23,55), East Sepik climbed from 221,9k to 631,8k around Wewak (37.825 in 2011) and middle Sepik floodplain villages, and border province West Sepik (Sandaun) tripled from 114,2k to 362,7k around Vanimo (13.970 in 2011) and Aitape [@fyfe2009gender; @guinea20132011].

Third stands the Southern (Papuan) region at 2,32M inhabitants (23,1% of the PNG ledger), defined by the starkest urban–rural density contrast in Melanesia. On just 338,7 km², the National Capital District (Port Moresby) multiplied more than sixfold from 123.624 in 1980 to 254.158 in 2000, 364.125 in 2011 and 756.754 in 2024—reaching 2.234,29 inhabitants per km² as squatter settlements expanded rapidly across Six Mile, Eight Mile, Sabama and Gerehu [@group2014papua; @ige2023counting; @guinea20252024]. Surrounding Central Province tripled from 117k to 373,8k (10,16 per km²), maritime Milne Bay rose from 128k to 412,2k around Alotau (11.857 in 2011), and Northern (Oro) expanded from 77,4k to 274k around Popondetta (12.600) and oil-palm estates. By contrast, vast sago-swamp and savanna lowlands remained PNG's emptiest interior frontier: Gulf held just 203,5k across 38.316,8 km² (5,31 per km²) and immense Western Province held 300k across 103.152,4 km² (2,91 per km²), concentrated around Daru (15.142), Kiunga (10.981) and Ok Tedi mining hub Tabubil (10.270) [@guinea20132011; @baxi2024how].

Fourth stands the New Guinea Islands region at 1,48M inhabitants (14,7% of the PNG ledger), combining high plantation productivity with post-disaster recovery. East New Britain expanded from 133,2k in 1980 to 434,8k in 2024 despite the 1994 Rabaul eruption, as Tolai cocoa farmers and provincial services shifted onto the Gazelle Peninsula plateau around Kokopo [@guinea2002papua; @guinea20252024]. Oil-palm resettlement schemes in West New Britain quadrupled provincial numbers from 88,9k in 1980 to 368,6k in 2024 and turned Kimbe into PNG's fastest-growing secondary town (1.172 in 1971 to 22.923 in 2011). New Ireland rose from 66k to 237,8k buoyed by Lihir gold royalties, small maritime Manus grew from 26k to 69,6k around Lorengau (8.882), and the Autonomous Region of Bougainville rebounded powerfully after the 1998 ceasefire—more than doubling from 175,2k in 2000 to 249,4k in 2011 and 367,1k in 2024 [@guinea20132011; @guinea20252024].

## Indonesian Papua Across Six Post-2022 Provinces (1971 to 2023)

West of the border, Indonesian Papua grew even faster than Papua New Guinea—multiplying sixfold over half a century from 923,4k in 1971 (898,5k summed across the back-apportioned provincial cache) to 3,59M in 2010, 5,44M in 2020 and 5,62M in 2023 (compounding at 3,53% per annum across 1971–2023 and 4,23% across 2010–2020 before moderating to 1,1% across 2020–2023 as post-pandemic administrative registration aligned with SP2020) [@papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil; @elmslie2010west]. Table \ref{tab:idn-provinces} displays the six post-2022 provinces across 1971, 2010, 2020 and 2023 alongside closing densities.

The six-province partition throws the ethnic and ecological divide of western New Guinea into sharp relief [@ananta2016statistics; @indonesia2021hasil]. Together, the two interior cordillera provinces account for exactly half (50,2%) of Indonesian Papua's population despite lacking deep-water ports or extensive state transmigration estates. *Papua Pegunungan* (55.566,5 km²) is the most populous province in Indonesian Papua at 1.464.466 inhabitants in 2023 (density 26,36 per km²), centred on the fertile Grand Baliem Valley around Wamena (rising from 6.400 in 1971 to 68.200 in 2023) and populous highland regencies of Jayawijaya, Yahukimo (Dekai), Lanny Jaya (Tiom), Tolikara (Karubaga), Nduga (Kenyam) and Pegunungan Bintang (Oksibil), where Indigenous Dani, Lani, Yali and Mek communities exceed 95% of residents [@ananta2016statistics; @papua2011penduduk]. Immediately west, *Papua Tengah* (59.960,2 km²) holds 1.357.071 inhabitants (density 22,63 per km²), fusing two contrasting worlds: the Indigenous Mee, Moni and Damal highlands around Enarotali (Paniai), Waghete (Deiyai), Mulia (Puncak Jaya) and Sugapa (Intan Jaya) on the north slope, and two major migrant-heavy hubs on the coast and southern foothills—transmigration-shaped provincial capital Nabire (7.200 in 1971 to 104.300 in 2023) and the Freeport mining conurbation of Timika (148.900) plus Tembagapura (23.022) [@mahmudah2023pemertahanan; @indonesia2021hasil].

Along the northern and western littorals, migration-driven coastal urbanisation dominates three provinces. Rump *Papua* (95.291,9 km²) holds 1.085.281 inhabitants (density 11,39), heavily concentrated around the Jayapura–Sentani metropolitan corridor (Kota Jayapura 414.862 in 2023 plus airport satellite Sentani 71.174 in 2020, together approaching half the province) alongside Cenderawasih Bay islands Biak (peaking at 51.800 in 2000 before settling at 43.728 in 2020 after inter-island air transit shifted away) and Serui (42.512) [@papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil]. On the western Bird's Head peninsula, *Papua Barat Daya* (48.244,5 km²) holds 613.180 inhabitants (density 12,71), overwhelmingly anchored by the oil, shipping and commercial gateway of Kota Sorong (23.800 in 1971 to 295.809 in 2023) and its fast-growing transmigration suburb Aimas (42.014 in 2020), where Bugis, Buton, Makassar, Moluccan and Javanese migrants have formed a commercial majority since the 1990s [@saprillah2011migrasi; @ananta2016statistics]. Adjacent *Papua Barat* (73.323,5 km²) holds 565.805 residents (density 7,72), centred on historic colonial and Otsus capital Manokwari (21.400 in 1971 to 102.400 in 2023), LNG hub Bintuni (32.590 in 2020), Kaimana (39.340) and nutmeg port Fakfak (18.824 in 2020 after regency boundary adjustments from 33.174 in 2010) [@indonesia2021hasil; @badanpusatstat2018indonesia]. Finally, southern lowland *Papua Selatan* (119.866 km²) remains Indonesian Papua's sparsest province at 533.910 inhabitants (density 4,45), pairing the Javanese rice-colonisation hub of Merauke (16.800 in 1971 to 108.470 in 2023) with tidal-swamp Indigenous river settlements at Kepi in Mappi (33.287), Agats in Asmat (23.869) and Tanah Merah in Boven Digoel (22.002) [@kamun2016kajian; @pona2012transmigrasi].

## Dual-State Urban Hierarchy and Rank-Size Structure

Even though New Guinea is split politically down the 141st meridian, its combined urban network conforms with striking precision to classic Zipf rank-size scaling, displayed in Figure \ref{fig:ng-hierarchy}. Across the upper half of the 145 catalogued centres (ranks 1 to 72, spanning Port Moresby at 756.754 down to Manam at 5.100), log-log regression yields $\alpha = 1,13$ with $R^2 = 0,98$ ($\alpha = 1,14$, $R^2 = 0,98$ excluding Sorong suburb Aimas; full 145-centre slope $-1,62$, $R^2 = 0,90$ reflecting the steep tail of small mission and patrol stations below 5k).

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:ng-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-modern-new-guinea/modern_new_guinea_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:ng-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Twelve largest catalogued urban centres across Papua New Guinea and Indonesian Papua by peak recorded population (Panel A) and rank-size distribution across 145 settlements with upper-half power-law fit ($\alpha = 1,13$, $R^2 = 0,98$ across the top 72 centres, Panel B), 1962 to 2024.</figcaption>
</figure>

Beneath the smooth island-wide power law, however, sits a dramatic cross-border asymmetry in urbanisation. Papua New Guinea remains one of the least urbanised countries on Earth: only two PNG cities—Port Moresby (756,8k in 2024) and Lae (148,9k in 2011)—appear among New Guinea's twelve largest recorded settlements, while ten of the top twelve sit inside Indonesian Papua: Jayapura (414,9k), Sorong (295,8k), Timika (148,9k), Merauke (108,5k), Nabire (104,3k), Manokwari (102,4k), Sentani (71,2k), Wamena (68,2k), Biak (51,8k) and Serui (42,5k) [@guinea20132011; @indonesia2021hasil]. Indonesian district *pemekaran* converted dozens of small *kecamatan* capitals into well-funded regency seats with salaried bureaucracies, paved airfields and migrant trader quarters, pushing Indonesian Papua's urban share past 30% while PNG's secondary provincial capitals—Wewak (37,8k), Madang (36k), Mount Hagen (29,8k), Kimbe (22,9k) and Goroka (22,8k)—remained modest market towns ringed by dense customary-tenure rural villages [@group2014papua; @bourke2009food].

# Limitations

Five structural constraints govern interpretation of modern New Guinea's demographic archive from 1962 to 2025.

First, Papua New Guinea's national census reliability deteriorated markedly after 2000 [@guinea20132011; @tatem2022high; @ige2023counting]. Incomplete post-enumeration surveys in 2011, a thirteen-year intercensal gap prolonged by COVID-19 and fiscal delays until 2024, urban informal-settlement undercount and political distortion in contested highland electorates leave a genuine +/-8% uncertainty envelope around PNG's 2024 total of 10,19M, even though remote-sensing extrapolations near 17M clearly over-count multi-structure rural Melanesian compounds [@tatem2022high; @guinea20252024]. Furthermore, vital registration remains fragmentary across rural districts, forcing reliance on indirect census orphanhood, DHS birth histories and sentinel verbal autopsies to track mortality [@bakker1986mortality; @kitur2019estimating; @hart2020mortality].

Second, within our 28-province constant-boundary cache, Western Highlands mirrors Western Province's census series (300.019 in 2024 against 462.566 in the official NSO final release), creating a documented 162,5k understatement in the PNG ledger total (10.022.816 versus 10.185.363 official). Readers citing Western Highlands specifically should consult the official NSO figures reported in Testing and Validation alongside Table \ref{tab:png-provinces} [@guinea20132011; @guinea20252024].

Third, in Indonesian Papua, administrative *pemekaran*—first from one province into two in 2003 and then into six in 2022, accompanied by a fourfold proliferation of regencies (*kabupaten*)—creates non-trivial boundary discontinuities for both provincial back-projections to 1971 and urban *distrik* time series [@papua2011penduduk; @indonesia2021hasil]. BPS SP2020's transition toward civil-registration (*Dukcapil*) hybrid enumeration also generated apparent step changes in remote highland regencies between 2010 and 2020, and our 2010–2020 two-province HGIS panel exhibits transitional polygon over-aggregation (5,67M and 8,61M) superseded by the clean six-province BPS reconciliation in 2023–2025.

Fourth, Papua New Guinea's 2024 census had released final provincial figures (including unified Port Moresby in the National Capital District at 756.754) prior to municipal town disaggregation; consequently, secondary PNG towns such as Lae, Wewak, Madang, Mount Hagen, Kimbe and Goroka hold 2011 as their latest documented town-level census benchmark in our gazetteer, understating their true 2024 urban footprints relative to Indonesian cities updated through 2023 [@guinea20132011; @guinea20252024].

Fifth, ethnic composition trends in Indonesian Papua cannot be tracked directly from SP2020 because BPS omitted the detailed ethnicity module fielded in SP2010; assessments of the Indigenous Papuan versus migrant demographic balance after 2010 therefore rely on SP2010 ethnic baselines combined with provincial-level highland versus coastal growth differentials [@ananta2016statistics; @elmslie2010west; @badanpusatstat2018indonesia].

# Conclusion

Between 1962 and 2025, New Guinea completed a sweeping demographic ascent that lifted its divided population from roughly 2,9M at the close of Dutch rule and 3,41M in 1971 to 15,81M official inhabitants (15,64M across our 28-province constant-boundary ledger) by 2023–2025 [@repository1982population; @guinea20252024; @indonesia2021hasil]. Rarely have two halves of a single landmass achieved comparably rapid growth through such contrasting mechanisms. Independent Papua New Guinea expanded almost exclusively by domestic natural increase—compounding at 2,81% per annum from 3,01M in 1980 to 10,19M in 2024—anchored by enduring rural fertility above four births per woman across its densely settled Highland valleys while rapid informal migration multiplied Port Moresby more than sixfold to 756,8k [@bourke2009food; @guinea2019papua; @group2014papua]. Indonesian Papua compounded even faster at 3,53% per annum from 923,4k in 1971 to 5,62M in 2023, combining state *transmigrasi*, spontaneous archipelagic commerce and Freeport mineral booms in coastal cities (Jayapura 414,9k, Sorong 295,8k, Timika 148,9k, Merauke 108,5k, Nabire 104,3k and Manokwari 102,4k) with dense Indigenous Papuan persistence across the highland cordillera of Papua Pegunungan (1,46M) and Papua Tengah (1,36M) [@elmslie2010west; @ananta2016statistics; @pona2012transmigrasi].

As the island enters the second quarter of the twenty-first century, its spatial architecture stands sharply defined: an extraordinarily tight cross-border rank-size urban curve ($\alpha = 1,13$, $R^2 = 0,98$) masking a much higher level of secondary-city urbanisation west of the 141st meridian than east of it, persistent rural public-health deficits across interior valleys, and a youthful population structure that ensures New Guinea will remain Oceania's dominant demographic engine for decades to come [@bauze2012equity; @kitur2020mortality; @baxi2024how].

# Footnotes

All numerical values follow European decimal conventions (comma decimals and dot thousands separators) paired with semantic magnitude abbreviations (k for thousands, M for millions). Constant-boundary provincial tables maintain the 28-unit partition (22 Papua New Guinea provinces including the National Capital District and Autonomous Region of Bougainville plus Indonesia's six post-2022 Papua provinces) across 1.007.772,1 km² of rasterised landmass and coastal archipelago mask area. Provincial enumerations draw directly on Papua New Guinea National Statistical Office censuses (1966–2024) and Badan Pusat Statistik Indonesia Sensus Penduduk and regional registrations (1971–2023).
